# 13-aircaps: sources

Back-test entry `13-aircaps.yaml`. AirCaps, YC Fall 2025 (Launch YC 2025-11-05). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **SITE**: https://www.aircaps.com (testimonials, pricing, how it works)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Olk-aircaps-the-ai-copilot-for-in-person-conversations
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/aircaps
- **YALE**: Yale Alumni Magazine. https://yalealumnimagazine.org/articles/6208
- **SD**: Stanford Daily, 2023-02-06 (TranscribeGlass). https://stanforddaily.com/2023/02/06/stanford-startup-transcribeglass-seeks-to-bring-ease-and-affordability-to-assistive-technology/
- **SMI**: Smithsonian Magazine. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/this-augmented-reality-tool-could-change-communication-for-some-deaf-and-hearing-impaired-people-180982996/
- **T4G**: Tech4Good Awards finalist entry. https://tech4goodawards.com/finalist/transcribeglass/ (quoted through the shortlist; not re-fetched)
- **HT**: HearingTracker, "Hear with Your Eyes: A Review of Live Captioning Glasses". https://www.hearingtracker.com/hearing-glasses/hear-with-your-eyes-five-ar-live-captioning-glasses
- **DTS-ASL**: ASL Deafined blog, "Dinner Table Syndrome: What Deaf, DeafBlind, and Hard of Hearing People Face". https://blog.asldeafined.com/2025/05/dinner-table-syndrome-what-deaf-deafblind-and-hard-of-hearing-people-face/

**Caution:** the origin story comes from the founder's earlier device, TranscribeGlass (about 2017 to 2023), which predates the YC batch. Here it is the founder's own account of where the problem came from, not evidence about AirCaps' buyers.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the CONSUMER role, `wearer`; context actor).**
- T4G (through the shortlist): a hard-of-hearing friend who "dropped out of school because day-to-day communication with other students was becoming an insurmountable problem".
- SMI: the friend "found it difficult to understand what teachers and even his friends were saying."
- YALE: the founder began at 16, after a hard-of-hearing classmate in Delhi left school because hearing aids alone did not let him follow his teachers (as read).
- SITE, "Who it's for": "Deaf and Hard of Hearing people" first, then travelers, multilingual families and professionals.

**2. What (the job).**
- YC-L: phones break eye contact and earbuds confuse the audio (as read), so face-to-face conversations get no captions.
- SITE: a private display in the lenses shows the text, visible only to the wearer (as read).
- Job wording ("follow and join a face-to-face conversation") is mine, from these two.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "When I was sitting around a table, I lost the conversation".
- SD (co-founder with hearing loss): "my understanding drops to 20% at best" in group conversations, where he mostly nods along.
- SMI: "Hearing aids aren't dependable in a lot of situations, especially ones with a lot of background noise."
- *My choice:* occasion "group conversation"; window 7 days; Frequency 4 to 7 days out of 7. That rests on YC-L's power users (6+ hours of daily use, as read) and the ordinary weekly rhythm of meals, work and family.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- SITE lists deaf and hard-of-hearing people first. YC-L also names meeting-heavy professionals.
- YALE: a Deaf ASL instructor who does not speak sees the glasses as one-directional.
- *My choice:* the segment is narrowed to "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week". This is the day-one wedge the origin story points at, and the travellers and professionals came later. Market US: the testimonials and HSA/FSA are US.

**5. Who pays (Buyer and payer).**
- SITE: "HSA/FSA eligible" (as read). One testimonial is from a daughter about her father joining family conversations.
- *My choice:* the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree (Nobody else, picked).

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- YC-L: captions and notes "displayed on lightweight AR glasses" (as read).
- SITE: four microphones capture nearby speech; the glasses "require a Bluetooth connection to a phone and an internet connection" (as read).
- Compatibility tests "Their phone was with them and online", because the mechanism needs both. Adoption friction tests "Wear the glasses, paired to the phone". Both are my choices from these facts.
- Commitment step "order a pair with free returns": SITE, "15-day risk-free returns".

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- SITE: glasses "Starting at $599"; free plan with unlimited captions; "Pro plan: $20/month".
- YALE: "which cost $649 in early 2026". HT's table: "$499 / $699 (Premium $20/mth)".
- *My choice:* the price is put on a year, because the ladder has no one-off: **$599 to $839 a year**. That is the glasses with free captions, up to the glasses plus twelve months of Pro.
- *My choice:* the cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$200 to $1,500 a year**, from the commercial statement's "many already pay for captioning apps and hearing-aid extras". No source gives a figure. SMI notes hearing aids are "often costing thousands of dollars", so the high end stops short of a hearing aid itself. Ability to pay is derived by code: 40% to 420%, some from spend.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- SITE testimonials: "I could start going to the theatre again"; "With AirCaps I can follow almost all" (at a table with friends); "I can attend speeches and seminars in large spaces and understand words"; a testimonial about an uncaptioned movie theater; one about a father following family conversations.
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups".
- YALE: a first-year deaf in one ear followed three friends in a noisy café. A largely deaf professor found the captions "messing up" at a screening, and they kept him in the loop on a walk drowned by construction noise.

## The respondents

No respondent carries a real person's name; every name is invented. Where a story follows a public account, the occasion is borrowed and the person is not.

- Harriet Coleman: SITE theatre testimonial ("I could start going to the theatre again").
- Walter Nguyen: shortlist reading of SITE ("My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups") and the SITE family-conversation testimonial.
- Diego Herrera: SITE table-with-friends testimonial; DTS-ASL ("if others are facing away or talking too quickly, these visual cues can be lost").
- Amaka Obi: YC-L (phones break eye contact); SMI (phone subtitles leave users "stuck looking at their screens at all times"); SITE work testimonial.
- Ruth Feldman: SITE testimonial on "speeches and seminars in large spaces".
- Tomás Reyes: YALE, the first-year deaf in one ear with three friends in a café.
- Eleanor Park: YALE, the campus walk where construction noise nearly drowned the conversation.
- Colette Marchand: SITE testimonial on an uncaptioned movie theater; YALE screening.
- Andrea Whitlock: YALE, the Deaf ASL instructor who sees the glasses as one-directional and worries institutions could cut services. She is the sceptic who will not adopt.
- Gordon McBride: author's invention, filling a gap: a hearing-aid user whose quiet week went fine, the low-frequency case. It is the other side of SMI's "aren't dependable ... with a lot of background noise".
- Kwame Asante: SD (bars: "I have a really hard time"; "my understanding drops to 20% at best", nodding along).
- Shirin Tehrani: SMI, the late-deafened user who relies "completely on live transcription and captions" and names doctor visits.
- Beatriz Souza: SMI ("Since the app needs the speaker to converse in English, I have not been able to use it much in social settings").
- Hollis Grant: author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, unanchored story so the entry carries one GUESSED reading.
- Naomi Adler: author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story (rather not say). DTS-ASL on "frustration, anxiety, and even a reluctance to attend social events".
- Frank Dellinger: DTS-ASL (family dinners and gatherings, "talking over each other").
- Ingrid Solberg: author's invention, filling a gap: a counter conversation through a screen and a mask, where lipreading fails. DTS-ASL on lost visual cues.
- Patrick Moran: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No (a quiet week with no hard conversation).
- Lucia Ferraro: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.
- Desmond Hale: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

## Open

- **The origin story predates the batch.** It is TranscribeGlass's. The day-one founder statements use it as the founders do in the press, but a back-test should weigh it as the founder's lived reason, not as customer evidence.
- **Price conflict.** SITE says $599, YALE $649 (early 2026), and HT $499 / $699. I used SITE's $599, as the price the founder would type today. The year framing ($599 to $839) is mine.
- **The cost estimate is mine.** $200 to $1,500 a year has no public figure behind it. The commercial vector's NOT_HOLDING_UP comes mostly from people who spend nothing today (free phone captions), against that estimate.
- **Two shortlist quotes not re-seen.** My fetch of SITE did not return the "sitting around a table, I lost the conversation" and "My wife appreciates..." quotes verbatim, though it did return the other testimonials. They are cited through the shortlist. The site may rotate testimonials.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The benefit is labelled "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" under the nearest code, `less_help_needed`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Frequency: many have it 2 to 3 days a week, not 4 to 7), SOLUTION HOLDING_UP, COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice).

screens.why7: Both rows are steps the wearer takes themselves, each under 9 words, in base form and in 'their' voice, with the daily charging habit included; but 'paired to the phone' leans on what Compatibility already tests (their phone with them and online), and the escape reads 'Leave this out of the study' rather than the card's 'I'm not sure'.
screens.instead: What will they have to do to start using it? (e.g. 'Wear the glasses through a whole conversation'; 'Charge the glasses every day') -- chip: I'm not sure

screens.why1: Right after I said what they'd have to do to start, it's obvious Keel shows me its list of those steps to check before I pick one to test.
screens.why2: 'Wear the glasses, paired to the phone' and 'Charge the glasses every day' are how I and my users talk about it, though the intro needlessly repeats the title.
screens.why3: Wearing, pairing and charging the glasses are things my wearers do themselves every day, so they can answer from their own week.
screens.why4: Two distinct efforts in my users' words, and the daily charge is the new habit I'd have missed, so nothing is odd or missing.
screens.why5: My row is kept as I wrote it and the belief says exactly what I typed.
screens.why7: Both are the wearer's own steps, on the one measure and in their voice, with my row first and Keel's suggested habit last, but my row bundles a one-time pairing with the habit of wearing glasses (a bundled-effort pitfall), its phone half edges toward what Compatibility tested, and the suggestion's why isn't shown.
screens.instead: Rows: 'Pair the glasses to their phone once' · 'Wear the glasses whenever they talk with people' · 'Charge the glasses every night' -- pick one to test.

screens.why1: Right after I checked the efforts Keel wrote from my answer, picking the one strangers get asked about is the obvious next step before the solution test is set.
screens.why2: Wearing the glasses, pairing them to the phone and charging them every day are exactly how I and my users talk about using AirCaps, so I read it once and picked.
screens.why3: I know which step loses people: getting someone to put on glasses paired to a phone and keep them on at the table, and the daily charge comes second.
screens.why4: Two distinct efforts: mine first, then Keel's daily-habit suggestion last, both in my own words, with nothing reworded and no step missing that I would pick instead.
screens.why5: My row is kept word for word, and the belief 'Most would wear the glasses, paired to the phone' is what I typed.
screens.why7: Both options are efforts the wearer takes themselves, and the belief can be supported or refuted by Yes / Only if / Probably not / No with I can't tell apart, but my row bundles wearing the glasses with keeping them paired to a phone, which leans on Compatibility's 'phone with them and online' rather than being one effort.
screens.instead: Which one is most likely to stop them? · Wear the glasses in conversations with hearing people · Charge the glasses every day

screens.why1: Asking whether to collect emails from people who say yes fits just before the study goes out to strangers, and it is a natural last setup step for me.
screens.why2: 'Pilot' is plain founder language, and the hint shows the exact line respondents will see and where I will find the yeses.
screens.why3: Whether I want early wearers to try the glasses is my own call, and I can answer it straight away.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers the choice, the two options are distinct, and no escape is needed for a decision that is mine.
screens.why5: Nothing I typed is changed; the screen only adds an opt-in line at the end of the study.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot? People who say yes see: "Would you try a pair for real, with 15-day free returns? Leave your email." (Yes, ask them / No pilot)

screens.why1: Picking an interviewer belongs just before the study goes out, but choosing a voice for deaf and hard-of-hearing adults comes abruptly, with no word on whether the video is captioned or signed.
screens.why2: The question and the two named voices with a preview are plain to me on first reading.
screens.why3: I can judge a voice by ear, but many of my respondents will never hear it, so the choice that matters for them (captions, readable text, maybe an ASL option) is one I would have to guess at.
screens.why4: Two voices are distinct and easy to preview, but there is no option for my audience, such as text-only or a captioned or signing interviewer, and no 'no preference' chip.
screens.why5: My answer was to lock the face Keel preselects, while the screen frames the pick as a voice, so it has drifted a little from what I chose.
screens.instead: How should deaf or hard-of-hearing adults get your questions? Captioned video with Daphne (picked for you) / Captioned video with Saskia / Text only, no video

screens.why1: Right after choosing who asks the questions, it is obvious I now pick how my respondents take them, and for deaf and hard-of-hearing adults that choice matters a lot.
screens.why2: Video interviewer, read and tap, or let them pick is plain to me, and the line that every question is also written on screen answers the first thing I would worry about.
screens.why3: I know how my people take in a conversation, and whether a spoken video interviewer suits them, so I can answer from what I know.
screens.why4: The three options are complete and distinct, but Daphne is described as asking aloud first and written second, which reads backwards for a deaf audience where the text is the main channel.
screens.why5: It uses my plural, deaf and hard-of-hearing adults, and keeps my pick of Read and tap without changing anything I typed.
screens.instead: How should deaf and hard-of-hearing adults answer? Options: Read and tap (they read each question and tap or type); AI interviewer Daphne, captioned (every question shown as text, with her voice and face on video for those who want them); Let them choose.

screens.why1: Right after choosing how people answer, deciding who gets the link is the obvious last step before sending.
screens.why2: Plain words; 'Contacts page' is Keel's own term but explained in place, and the three choices read on first pass.
screens.why3: I know whether I'm sending to deaf and hard-of-hearing users I know by name, a list I built, or a community group like a Facebook or HLAA forum.
screens.why4: The three options are distinct and cover my real channels, but the open-link option's Google sign-in is an odd detail to bundle into the choice, and a mix of named people plus a community post has no option.
screens.why5: Nothing of my study is touched here; my pick of people I know by name stands as typed.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? People I know by name (each their own link) / A list from Keel's Contacts page / One open link I post in a group where they already are (e.g. an HLAA chapter or Deaf community forum) -- and let me pick more than one.

screens.why_b1: The verdict "Holding up" sits under the title with "3 beliefs: 3 holding" right beside it, and each card shows its count against its bar (7 of 7, bar 5 of 7), so I know it held and by how much.
screens.why_b2: Each card line says what was counted (said yes, would have gone better, would do it), over 7 people, and where my bar sits (5 of 7), though "yes or yes, with some steps" reads clumsily.
screens.why_b3: Compatibility, Relative advantage and Adoption friction carry my three belief lines word for word as I checked them, even if Keel's solution statement above them is garbled ("wearing the glasses the app on lightweight glasses... and gets back live captions").
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what to do next, such as moving to the commercial stage or probing the 3 who would only wear them on a condition; "What it measures" only explains the rule.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible, but 7 of 7 on every belief is shown with no word that seven is a small sample, and the 3 conditional adopters are counted as "would do it" with no caveat.
screens.instead: Holding up on all three, but from only 7 people: 3 of the 7 would wear the glasses only on a condition, so read those conditions next, then go to the commercial stage, where the price is the open question.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "7 of 7 said yes or yes, with some steps · bar 5 of 7", so I see the verdict and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the answers to the phone question (Yes 4, Yes with some steps 3, No 0) over 7 people, and the strip puts the marker at 5 of 7, so all three are plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: The card is titled Compatibility and the belief line is word for word the one I checked, though the asked line underneath ("Had your phone with you and online?") is clipped and has no subject.
screens.why_b4: The So line tells me concretely that phone and connection won't be what stops my wearers, and it sends me to Adoption friction as the thing to look at next.
screens.why_b5: The count line rightly calls 7 people a lean and not a call, but the So line then says flatly that the phone "is not what will stop them" and that adoption friction "is", which is firmer than seven answers carry; the three quotes filed under Compatibility (a matinee trial, audience questions, a noisy walk) aren't about the phone at all.
screens.instead: Seven of seven had their phone with them and online, so on this small group the phone and data link look unlikely to block AirCaps; check Adoption friction next. The comments here are about trying a pair first, so file them there.

screens.why_b1: The verdict and its deciding number sit side by side: 'Holding up', '7 of 7 said it would have gone better', against a bar of 5 of 7, and they agree.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts 'better' answers, all 7 a lot and none a little, over 7 people, with my bar marked at 5 of 7, so I can read it at first look even though the against side is only implied by its absence.
screens.why_b3: The card is titled Relative advantage and carries my benefit word for word, 'following more without asking anyone to repeat', the same awkward line I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: The So line mostly restates the count and then hands the open question to Adoption friction, without saying what this means for the idea, for example that the advantage is strong enough to lead with and the risk is wearing the glasses.
screens.why_b5: n stays at 7 throughout, the screen calls it 'a lean, not a call', and it flags the answers as a hypothetical asked with AirCaps in mind, so nothing claims more than the 7 can carry.
screens.instead: All 7 said a lot better, so the advantage itself isn't the risk and you can lead with it; but 7 is a lean, and the open question is whether they'd wear the glasses paired to the phone (Adoption friction, below).

screens.why_b1: The verdict, Holding up, sits right beside the deciding number, 7 of 7 against a bar of 5 of 7, and they agree.
screens.why_b2: At first look I can see it counts answers to the wear-and-pair question, over 7 people, with the marker at 5 and every cell for me.
screens.why_b3: Adoption friction and 'Most would wear the glasses, paired to the phone' are exactly what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: The So line promises that what would make it worth it to the 3 conditional people is below, but nothing below names their condition; the one quote is Tomás on taking the end seat, a workaround rather than a catch, so I still don't know if the snag is battery, comfort, looks or the phone pairing.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible, the count line splits 4 as is from 3 on a condition, and it says a small group gives a lean, not a call, so the 7 of 7 is not oversold.
screens.instead: Say what each of the 3 'only if' people would need (all-day battery, comfort over hearing aids, a phone that stays paired), or drop the 'below' promise and say their condition wasn't captured.

screens.why_b1: Each box states the verdict, 'Compatibility held, 7 of 7' and 'Adoption friction held, 7 of 7', and puts the bar of 5 of 7 right beside it, so I know both lines held and by how much.
screens.why_b3: Both belief lines are word for word the ones I checked on the way in: phone with them and online, and wear the glasses paired to the phone.
screens.why_b4: The screen lists what people added but never says what it means for AirCaps; it does not say that people want to try the glasses in their own hard setting before buying, or that a big hall needs audience pickup, so I am left to work out the next step myself.
screens.why_b5: The 7 of 7 counts are honest and n is visible, but nothing says seven is a small group, and 'held, 7 of 7' sits above quotes about demos and big halls that say nothing about a phone being with them and online.
screens.why_b6: The quotes add three things I did not type: people want to borrow a pair and test it on their own noisy walk or matinee before ordering, even with 15-day returns; a seminar-goer needs audience questions picked up, not just the speaker; and a one-sided-deaf student's end-seat trick is the free workaround I am really competing with.
screens.instead: Held 7 of 7 (a small group of seven); three wanted to try a pair in their own hard setting first, so offer a demo or loan for one real occasion; one needs audience questions picked up in large halls; one gets by with an end seat, which is the habit you have to beat.

screens.why1: It's the first screen and checks I'm the right person before anything else, so it's obvious why it's asked.
screens.why2: 'Hearing people' is how deaf and hard-of-hearing people talk about everyone else, so it's plain to me on first read.
screens.why3: I know whether I talked with hearing people this week (at the shop, at work, with family), so I can answer from my own life.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, they don't overlap, and a gate question needs no escape.
screens.why5: Nothing about a product or a company's plan reaches me, and the words are ones I would use myself.
screens.why6: 'I'll read 2 options. Yes; or No.' is clunky for a plain yes-or-no question when the screener's spoken form should just be the question followed by 'Yes or no.'
screens.instead: Do you talk with hearing people every week? Yes or no.

screens.why1: Right after asking whether I talk with hearing people every week, asking whether I lost track of one of those conversations this week is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: "Lose track of a conversation" is exactly how I'd say it, and I can answer on first hearing.
screens.why3: I know whether I lost the thread at the shop, at work or at a family dinner this week, so I can answer from my own week.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it, and both are true of someone: some weeks I lose the thread, some weeks everyone faces me and speaks clearly.
screens.why5: Nothing about a product, a device or the company reaches me, only my own conversations in my own words.
screens.why6: It's one short question ending in "Yes or no," easy to take in at once.
screens.why7: The measure, the two fixed answers and their order, and the missing escape all fit, and a No is truly possible so the share can go either way, but the gate drops "face-to-face," so a phone or video call I lost track of would count as Yes when the founder counted only face-to-face talk.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did you lose track of a face-to-face conversation with hearing people? Yes · No

screens.why1: After asking whether I lost track of a conversation with hearing people this week, showing me an idea for following those conversations is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Captions, glasses and eye contact are words I use every day, and each sentence is short enough to take in on one read.
screens.why3: Missing words when I look down at a phone, and losing someone's face while I read, is exactly what my week is like, so I can judge this from my own life.
screens.why4: It is a card to read with no options.
screens.why5: The idea is shown on purpose as an Imagine card, and nothing in it names me or anyone else in words I wouldn't use.
screens.why6: Short plain sentences that say well aloud, though repeating 'lightweight glasses with the app on them' right after the first line sounds a little clumsy heard once.
screens.instead: Imagine AirCaps, an app on lightweight glasses that captions speech. When people near you talk, live captions of their words appear inside the lens. The people building it believe it would let you read the words while keeping eye contact.

screens.why1: Right after the glasses idea it jumps to my phone, and I only work out later that the glasses must run off it, so it feels abrupt.
screens.why2: "Had your phone with you and online?" is a broken half-sentence that asks two things at once, so if I had my phone but no signal I don't know what to say.
screens.why3: I know whether my phone was on me and had a signal the last time I talked with hearing people.
screens.why4: "Yes, with some steps" is odd for whether my phone was in my bag, because either it was or it wasn't, and the three options otherwise fit.
screens.why5: Nothing leaks beyond the idea card I was shown on purpose, and "phone" and "online" are my words.
screens.why6: Heard aloud, the stem with no subject sounds clipped and I'd have to replay it, though the three options and "you can't tell" are easy to hold.
screens.why7: The measure, the shape and the escape fit a fact's three options plus "I can't tell", but the condition joins two things (with you, and online), and almost everyone in this group always has their phone on them, so it is close to settled and could rarely count against; the step the idea rests on, wearing the glasses and reading captions while talking, is not tested.
screens.instead: On your last conversation with hearing people, could you have read captions on glasses while still watching their faces? Yes, easily · Yes, most of the time · Only sometimes · No · I can't tell

screens.why1: I'd just said my phone was with me and online only with some steps, so it makes sense to ask what those steps were.
screens.why2: It doesn't say back what I picked, and 'having your phone online' is not how I'd put it; I'd say 'getting my phone connected' or 'getting signal or wifi'.
screens.why3: I know exactly what I did, like finding the cafe wifi or turning data back on, so I can answer from my own week.
screens.why4: It's a box to type in, with no options.
screens.why5: It only asks about my phone being connected, which the idea card already set up, and nothing new about their product reaches me.
screens.why6: It's one short question that's easy to hear once and answer, though on the voice link I'd want it captioned.
screens.instead: You said your phone was online with some steps. What did you have to do to get it connected for that conversation?

screens.why1: Straight after the glasses card and the phone question, asking whether AirCaps would have helped is the obvious next thing to ask me.
screens.why2: I get it, but 'the last conversation when you had to follow and join a face-to-face conversation' says conversation twice and sounds like a form, not how I'd put it; I'd say 'keep up with what people were saying'.
screens.why3: I talk with hearing people every week and know exactly how my last one went, so I can judge whether captions in front of my eyes would have helped.
screens.why4: A lot better, a little better, no difference, worse, plus I can't tell covers every answer I could have, with no overlap.
screens.why5: Nothing leaks beyond the idea card I was shown on purpose; it just names the glasses and asks if they'd have helped.
screens.why6: The stem runs to about thirty words with the idea's description repeated mid-sentence, so by the time I hear 'or not?' I've had to hold a lot, though the four options say cleanly.
screens.why7: Measure, the fixed four in order, the 2-for-2-against balance and the lone I can't tell are all right, but the occasion is any last conversation rather than the hard one, too fast or too noisy to follow, where captions would be tested.
screens.instead: Think of the last time hearing people talked too fast or it was too noisy to follow. Would AirCaps have helped you keep up, or not? A lot better · A little better · No difference · Worse · I can't tell

screens.why1: After asking whether AirCaps would have done better for me, it makes sense to ask whether I'd actually put the glasses on and use them.
screens.why2: Wearing glasses paired to my phone is plain to me, since I pair hearing aids and earbuds to my phone all the time.
screens.why3: I know whether I'd wear captioning glasses in front of hearing people, so I can answer this from my own life.
screens.why4: 'Yes, if it was clearly worth it' is barely different from plain 'Yes' and hides my real catch, which is whether they'd go over my own prescription glasses or make me stand out in a conversation.
screens.why5: Only the idea card's own description reaches me, in words I'd use, and nothing of the founder's plan or roles leaks.
screens.why6: It's one short question with four short options and one escape, easy to hold when heard once.
screens.why7: Wearing the glasses paired to my phone is a step I take myself, all the options sit on one measure in the card's order with two for and two against, and I can't tell is the one escape; the plain conditional is the card's allowed fallback.
screens.instead: To use AirCaps, you'd wear the glasses, paired to your phone. Would you do that, or not? Yes · Only if they worked with my own glasses · Probably not · No · I can't tell

screens.why1: A closing question about what would win me over makes sense after the glasses question, but it doesn't follow on from what I just said about wearing them, and 'worth it' brings in cost that nobody has mentioned yet.
screens.why2: Short and in plain words, and it calls the thing AirCaps, the name I was just given, rather than a bare 'it' or a pasted description.
screens.why3: I can answer from my own life: captions that keep up in a noisy room, glasses I'd actually wear all day, a battery that lasts a dinner out.
screens.why4: A box to type in, with no options or chips.
screens.why5: AirCaps was named on purpose on the idea card, and nothing else of the founder's plan or terms comes through here.
screens.why6: One short question that is easy to hear once and answer.
screens.instead: What would make you want to wear AirCaps the next time you're talking with hearing people?
